subject: English
central_question: How does the poem use an absurd chain of justice to expose foolish government and show why the people value peace and liberty above the ruler’s identity?
in_scope_units: The King orders a triumphal arch, but its low height knocks off his crown.
Responsibility is passed from the chief builder to the workmen, masons, architect and finally the King.
The wisest man blames the arch, while public impatience turns justice into a demand for any immediate hanging.
The King alone fits the noose and is executed by his own royal decree.
An idiot’s customary answer leads the ministers to crown a melon as the next ruler.
The citizens accept the Melon King because they retain peace and liberty.
The end questions develop narration, political interpretation, humour, irony and verse form.
banned_topics: Historical claims about an actual Melon City or king
Modern constitutional theory not discussed in the poem
Biographical details about Vikram Seth beyond the source introduction

known_pitfalls.claim: The King is a wise and fair ruler because he repeatedly calls himself just.
known_pitfalls.correction: His decisions are impulsive and contradictory; the repeated description “just and placid” is ironic.

known_pitfalls.claim: The architect is executed for the faulty arch.
known_pitfalls.correction: The blame returns to the King because he had altered the plans, and the King is eventually hanged because he alone fits the noose.

known_pitfalls.claim: The people choose the melon after careful political debate.
known_pitfalls.correction: The next passer-by is an idiot whose standard answer is “A melon,” and custom makes that answer binding.

known_pitfalls.claim: The poem praises complete political indifference.
known_pitfalls.correction: Its closing reference to laissez faire is satirical and must be read alongside the absurd administration.

known_pitfalls.claim: The humour is separate from the poem’s message.
known_pitfalls.correction: Humour and irony expose mechanical justice, fearful ministers and passive citizenship.

recommended_example_progression: Begin with NCERT Q1 by narrating the complete cause-and-effect chain in one’s own words.
Use NCERT Q2 to analyse the ironic description “just and placid.”
Use NCERT Q4 to identify humour and irony at the blame-shifting, hanging and coronation stages.
Conclude with NCERT Q3 and Q5 on peace, liberty and the charm of verse narration.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The poem ends with five numbered questions on narration, the state and its King, peace and liberty, humour and irony, and verse storytelling.
